item.title: Chinese Data Center Tied to Alice Huang Found Using Nvidia's Powerful AI Chips
item.description:
Friday Nvidia's stock showed a 30.95% drop over the last month, and a 37% drop from its October 2nd high of $239.24. But it managed a 4.83% gain for the week — after some bad news hit Friday morning... A Chinese data center with ties to Alice Huang (the suspected Chinese spy-agency asset) "has installed hardware with Nvidia's powerful Blackwell AI chips," writes Gizmodo, citing a Friday morning report from Bloomberg. Those chips are "among Nvidia's most powerful products," writes Bloomberg, and their presence was confirmed by "a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November," (offering the hardware as collateral for a $14 million loan, according to bank filings seen by Bloomberg News). A second Chinese company (this one controlled by a Tokyo-based parent company) also described a server with Nvidia's advanced Blackwell chips in documents for a similar loan in late 2025 from, Bloomberg reports: The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. [Alice Huang has ties to "a number of companies" that invested in the second company, and its president is her husband Kang Wei.] These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license. President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge... Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn't responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the partnership as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation." Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a "specific area" facility in an unnamed country... The parameters they've outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co. Bloomberg says Nvidia "has not answered repeated queries," though they add that Nvida "for years insisted that there was no black market for its products." The article also notes that Megaspeed (where Alice Huang worked) "won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation" in 2023, and went on to become Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: Mozilla Thanks Users For New Features in Firefox 161: Site-Specific VPN and Keyboard Shortcuts
item.description:
Firefox 161 (released Tuesday) promises "A better Firefox, thanks to you. All of these improvements began with a community request." In a Thanksgiving-themed message, they wrote "Here's to the passionate people who keep us moving forward." Choose which sites always open with VPN. Our free built-in VPN just got one of its most requested upgrades. Pick sites where the VPN always turns on, and sites where it stays off because they work better without it. Bonus: VPN data is unlimited through January. Use it as much as you like until then... Set your own shortcuts . Create keyboard shortcuts for what you use most, like opening tabs, saving pages or closing windows. Type "about:keyboard" in the address bar. See images appear as they load. Firefox now supports JPEG XL, an image format that lets you see a preview of the full image before it downloads. Neowin notes Firefox is also committing to its redesign: Mozilla has been trying to win over users from Chromium-based browsers, hoping they pick up Firefox. To do so, aside from still supporting uBlock Origin, the firm made a big design shift this year by introducing Nova, so that users on the other side can feel they are familiar with it, as it brings the more common, modern rounded corner design philosophy, which Google's Chrome has been using for quite a while... However, as is usually the case, not everyone has been on-board with Nova and they are completely fine to feel that way; Mozilla also understands this which is why it offered a way to opt-out of it by tweaking a configuration setting via about:config. However, this week the firm announced that it is going to take that option away. In a post on its official Mozilla Connect forum, which was shared with us by Neowin forum member ecmram, the Firefox team confirmed that it will remove the config toggle preference for reverting to the old design next month in December. The company says that the rollout of Nova is now complete, and it wants to lock the preference to ensure that Firefox performs as intended and to prevent unexpected browser behavior. As such, anyone who has previously used the browser.nova.enabled preference to disable the redesign will automatically get Nova starting next month, thus wiping the official way to return to the previous UI once the change takes effect. On the positive side, Mozilla is not entirely ignoring feedback from users who are unhappy with the redesign. The company says it has introduced several changes based on community feedback, including a new set of Classic Themes with the latest version 161, that offer flat colors without gradients. These can be found under about:addons, and one of them even mimics the older Proton design with a gray appearance. There is a new Fire toolbar button too that clears history with a single-click.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: Nvidia Seeded Pirated Books and Shared Them With Adobe, Authors Allege
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Several book authors have filed (PDF) an amended complaint accusing Nvidia of seeding pirated books via BitTorrent, after downloading them from shadow libraries including Anna's Archive and LibGen. [...] These tools can download files via BitTorrent, and the authors and Nvidia both agree that whether they also upload data to others depends on the settings used. According to the authors, Nvidia didn't prevent seeding altogether. "When Nvidia ran the BitTorrent client, Nvidia uploaded pieces of pirated book files to third parties during the downloading process (i.e., before the download was complete). Nvidia also 'seeded' pirated books (i.e., made available and uploaded parts of a completely downloaded file). While Nvidia took some steps to limit seeding, it did not prevent seeding altogether," the complaint reads. The authors say they found out in June, when Nvidia handed over the code it used for torrenting. Based on that code, they were "able to determine that Nvidia did not disable uploading," the authors told the court. The complaint states that the authors' own books were among those Nvidia downloaded. However, the claim that they were also uploaded to others is made "on information and belief," which essentially means the authors don't have direct knowledge of it. In addition to the seeding claims, the authors also allege that Nvidia shared the pirated books with business partners, including Adobe, through a "PDF Extraction Project" involving 250 million pages. These pages were acquired in part from shadow libraries such as Anna's Archive and LibGen. According to the complaint, Nvidia shared its pirated books with Adobe because it wanted to "get tokens out of PDFs to create differentiated models" and "include PDF extraction into our NeMo pipeline so that customers can leverage their PDF content." In return, the complaint says, Adobe committed to using Nvidia's language models in some of its products. That made the deal a big opportunity for Nvidia, with its NeMo AI models potentially "powering every one of Adobe PDFs," the authors write. Adobe wasn't the only partner. The complaint also mentions partnerships with Cohere and Imbue that involved sharing Nvidia's base training data and offering books acquired from shadow libraries. The authors believe their own books were shared with all three companies, but this is alleged on information and belief. With these allegations, the amended complaint now accuses Nvidia of distributing the books itself and of helping others to infringe, which falls under its existing direct and contributory infringement claims.

item.title: This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer
item.description:
When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.

At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.

Dinesh Rai


Employer:

Boston Children’s Hospital

Occupation:

Clinical AI Engineer

Education:

Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine

It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology.

Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.

When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.

Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”

For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.

Between medicine and engineering

Rai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.

For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.

His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.

That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.

At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job.

Uncovering “clinical doppelgangers”

One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.

The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.

Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.

Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.

Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.

Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.

Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.

“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”

After the prompt

In medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?

That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.

Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”

An evolving career

The evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.

What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.

That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles.

“The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

item.title: James T. Russell, Physicist Who Pioneered CD and DVD Technology, Dies At 95
item.description:
James T. Russell, the American physicist whose pioneering digital-to-optical recording and playback system laid the foundation for CD, DVD and Blu-ray technology, has died at the age of 95. "Russell never became a household name, but the technology he developed, later licensed by Sony and Phillips, would transform everything from the way people listen to music to the way data is stored," reports The Daily Chronicle. From the report: In a career spanning almost his entire life, Russell earned more than 70 patents, but his biggest breakthrough was the invention of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system in the 1960s and early 1970s, a system that brought crystal clear audio and film to the masses. [...] It was in Richland that Russell started exploring how to create cleaner recordings of music. Popping and hissing often accompanied the music of vinyl records, from the analog sound of a needle scraping against microgrooves, and Russell thought he could do something about it. He crunched the numbers before bringing an invention report to Battelle: What if a light beam could read a digital record? "It isn't clear what the problem was," Russell recalled in a Seattle Times interview in 2004. "I think there was some feeling amongst the moneybags that it probably wouldn't work, (or) if it did work there's no advantage, no value in optical records. What would you use it for, and would people want it and, anyway, if it was any good, IBM would have already invented it." While his idea faced skepticism early on, the company gave him some money to experiment. Russell invented an early method to store audio digitally and play it back to produce a flawless sound. He also created a way to store digital information densely. Other primitive, analog laser disk technology had been developed in the 1950s by engineer David Paul Gregg. Russell's earliest patents in the field were issued in the mid-1960s, with a working prototype finished by the 1970s, using a laser to read binary data on a compact disc, or CD. The patent for Russell's invention passed from company to company, bringing him from Richland to Salt Lake City, then to Toronto. His development of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system became foundational to CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-ray technology. Russell didn't earn royalties, never made a fortune, and was rarely credited for his work.

item.title: Scientists Used Seabirds To Track Hidden Ships
item.description:
Scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders and GPS trackers to detect fishing vessels that were not broadcasting their locations through the Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to a new study published in Science Advances. They found that unseen vessels accounted for about 32% of vessel-related audio detections in the North Atlantic and 12% in the Mediterranean. "The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off," adds 404 Media. From the report: Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship's location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons -- such as evading pirates -- or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming "bycatch" when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear. Unseen vessel activity "is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal," said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a "powerful tool for improving risk assessment" by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map.

item.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot To Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that's cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps. [...] Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks. "We've added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments," says Oscar O'Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. "This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much." O'Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free. In Anthropic's tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively. AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they're being tested. But O'Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test. As AI models get ever smarter, many researchers worry about whether they'll outwit their human counterparts. If that does happen, then it may be essential that agents -- and not just the executives responsible for them -- can resist temptation.

item.title: How Engineers Designed a Mission to One of Jupiter’s Icy Moons
item.description:
On 3 December 2026, a 30.5-meter-wide space probe will slingshot past Earth, picking up the speed it needs to reach Jupiter in 2030. The Europa Clipper is designed to investigate Jupiter’s enigmatic moon Europa and look for places that could support life in the ocean beneath the moon’s thick shell of ice. Tim Larson is the project manager for the mission at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and he spoke to IEEE Spectrum about designing and flying the Europa Clipper.

Tim Larson


Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years.

Why take such a roundabout route to Jupiter?

Tim Larson: That’s all driven by the energy that we got from our launch vehicle, the Falcon Heavy. It set a MEGA trajectory: Mars-Earth Gravity Assist. So about 4 months after launch, we flew by Mars, got an assist there. Now we’re coming back in for a final assist from Earth to get on our outbound trajectory to Jupiter.

The Europa Clipper is set to orbit Jupiter and fly by Europa about 50 times to study it. Why not just orbit it directly?

Larson: The big challenge is the radiation environment. It is so intense that any spacecraft orbiting Europa wouldn’t last very long. So the mission designers came through with this concept of the flybys.

We will be in a three-week orbit around Jupiter, but the orbit is synchronized so that every time we fly by Jupiter, Europa is right there. Over time, you build up the coverage of the surface that we’re ultimately after. We spend a relatively short time in the high-radiation environment, and then the rest of the orbit is in a more benign environment where we can relay data back down to Earth, et cetera.

The Europa Clipper relies on solar panels to generate power. Why not use a compact radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG)?

Larson: It’s a national policy to only use RTGs if it is absolutely essential. A lot of the early concepts that focused on orbiting Europa had to go with RTG approaches, because you’d spend so much time in the shadow of Jupiter. Once we shifted over to the flyby mission approach, it turned out solar arrays would be feasible.

How are Europa Clipper’s electronics different from other probes?

Larson: One of the things that we dealt with in our design was the level of radiation tolerance that we had to get in all our parts. In our main avionics module—we call it the vault—everything in there is designed to an exposure of 150 kilorads (1,500 sieverts). To get our usual factor-of-two margin, we were buying parts that rated to 300 kilorads.

That brings up side challenges, because when you buy high-radiation-tolerance versions of parts, you can’t always get the exact same part functionality. You might have to change your circuits a little bit. And they don’t always have the same form factor, so you have to accommodate that.

How do you preserve fine-grained technical knowledge about the spacecraft over its yearslong mission lifetime?

Larson: By the time we launch, we try to get everything documented. As we learn about the idiosyncrasies of the spacecraft, we capture that in databases. When we have personnel turnover, we try to have a lot of overlap. We’re looking at how AI can take in this broad array of information we have in multiple different formats and locations, and extract information.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “Tim Larson.”

item.title: Physicists Send an Unblockable Message Using Gravity
item.description:
Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from Phys.org: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, "Gravity." The research has been published in Science Advances. "Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," [said Dr. Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics]. "While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block." Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed. "Our elevator was snail-paced -- it's from the 1950s -- so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," White said. "The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector. Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters (1,640 feet) and data rates of around 15 bits per minute."

This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. "The CO2 increase from this year to next will be about 3.5 parts per million, a third faster than in recent years and nearly twice as fast as what it should have been limited to if we'd been on track to limit global warming to 1.5C." Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, said: "Another day, another global temperature record," adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been "smashed."

item.title: Suspected Chinese Agents Are Trying to Dupe Americans with Fake Listings on Job Platforms
item.description:
"LinkedIn is probably the greatest intelligence tool that's ever been created," CNN heard from Holden Triplett, director of counterintelligence at the National Security Council in the first Trump administration. A LinkedIn spokesperson responded that "Creating a fake account or misrepresenting your identity is a clear violation of our terms of service." (And they also told CNN that LinkedIn remains "focused on detecting state-sponsored abuse and will continue to enforce our policies against fake accounts.") But it's not just happening on LinkedIn... Suspected Chinese spies have created an elaborate web of fake firms with job opportunities aimed at tricking current and former US officials into divulging government secrets as part of a scheme that is more pervasive than previously reported, CNN has found. Interviews with a dozen people caught up in the operation — as well as CNN analysis of suspected bogus websites — reveal how there is a much broader target pool for obtaining sensitive US information after the Trump administration laid off thousands of federal employees. [CNN reported in 2025 that "foreign powers such as China and Russia" had directed their intelligence services "to ramp up recruiting of Americans working in national security by targeting those who had been fired or felt they were at risk of losing their jobs".] These workers left their posts with inadequate guidance and protection from spying plots, ex-officials said, creating a potentially valuable resource for Beijing and weak spot for Washington... In addition to government workers, the plot has targeted journalists, trade consultants and others, who might have knowledge deemed valuable to US adversaries. The FBI offered a glimpse into the malicious recruiting scam when it seized 13 websites officials say were tied to fake consulting firms in June. China denied the FBI allegations. CNN analyzed the sites' software code, looked at other suspicious job listings, and interviewed people approached by similar companies. CNN identified several more websites that mimicked the style and substance of those disabled by the FBI. Two more sites that Max Lesser, a senior analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank, discovered and shared with CNN have some of the same web infrastructure or other connections to the seized websites. In total, Lesser has uncovered more than 100 other web domains, many of which share similar characteristics with the sites taken down by the FBI.... This sprawling network has the hallmarks of a Chinese intelligence operation, Lesser told CNN. After creating fake web sites, the operatives "plant vague, well-paying job ads for consulting positions focused on China-related issues" on jobs sites like LinkedIn, CNN reports, asking applicants to produce "research reports". ("[D]ozens or hundreds of such reports, across various topics of interest to Beijing, can start to form a much clearer picture of US national security policy and its vulnerabilities, according to current and former FBI officials.") CNN sent a detailed request for a comment to a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC. "I am not familiar with what you mentioned," they responded, adding that China "opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called 'Chinese spy' narrative."

item.description:
CNN published an exclusive report Tuesdayon what caused last week's nationwide ground stop for flights in the U.S.. Investigators have focused on determining why a new router at a remote Arkansas radio site overwhelmed the nation's air traffic control system with a massive amount of data, triggering gaps in radar and radio communications. item.title: Those Five Tons of Bomb-Making Chemicals in Iowa Will Be Detonated Wednesday Morning
item.description:
The detonation is back on. Nearly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives will be detonated Wednesday morning at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, reports the Iowa Capital Dispatch (part of the nonprofit States Newsroom network "The scheduled time follows numerous delays over the past week from the Army, a lawsuit, intervention from the president, and widespread public concern of the health and environmental effects associated with detonating a lead-based explosive." Lead deposition maps released by the Army Tuesday morning show lead released by the detonation could be dispersed in the air as far as 100 miles southwest of Middletown and cross into Missouri. An additional map shows there is a potential for lead surface dust to settle as far as 50 miles southwest of the detonation site. The Army has recommended, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency is supporting, the evacuation of Iowans in Middletown and the immediate area — a 5-mile cone to the southwest of the detonation site — during the detonation period. Soldiers, environmental teams and other federal officials are in the area helping to sample soils and alert residents of the detonation plans... A slew of federal officials from the Army, the EPA, Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, Department of Agriculture and more gathered at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant Tuesday for a press conference and shared new information with the public about the response... Speaking at the press conference Tuesday, Sean Kaufman with HHS said the highest risk is for pregnant individuals, children, or people with chronic illnesses who live or plan to be in the areas the Army forecasts will be impacted. "You definitely want to be out of that area," Kaufman said of the at-risk groups. "I would evacuate that area that's signaled in the model... " As many as 100 Iowa National Guard soldiers will be available to aid local, state and federal agencies in their public safety plans [according to a news release from the governor]. They will also help provide guidance and assistance to around 150 households with a temporary evacuation... At the news conference, acting Secretary of the Army Hon. Adam Telle emphasized that the government's priority was the "health and safety of the citizens of this region." Telle said those involved have sought advice from "every expert" in and outside of the federal government and have considered all viable options and data before reaching the conclusion to proceed with detonation. "There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, is far preferable to an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said. Some of those mitigations include: sand around the structure holding the barrels; two walls of four, 16,000-gallon water tanks; a plan to "flood" the exterior of the storage area with aqueous foam to help absorb particulate matter from the blast; and modeling to forecast impacted areas based on weather conditions.

item.title: New PET tracer cocktail rapidly detects hospital-acquired bacterial infections
item.description: A novel radiotracer cocktail can accurately identify multiple strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa—a leading cause of hospital-acquired infections—within hours, according to new research published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine. By targeting multiple strains of the bacteria, this rapid detection approach has the potential to enable targeted therapy and reduce the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics among critically ill patients.

item.title: Amber fossils reveal how grasshoppers may have walked on water 100 million years ago
item.description: Walking on water represents one of the most striking modes of locomotion in the natural world and plays a crucial role in animals' colonization of ecological niches at the water surface. However, insects specialized for this locomotion (obligate surface dwellers) belong to only two groups: the living Gerromorpha (Hemiptera) and extinct Chresmodidae (stem group of Polyneoptera). Elucidating how extinct insects moved on the water surface has proven highly challenging, and the adaptive evolution of different insect lineages to ecological niches at the water surface remains poorly understood.

item.title: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
item.description: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function and increase the risk of hospitalization and premature death.
